title: If–Then Decoder
goal: Spot the signal word, put each side where it belongs, and say whether the order flips. Fast.
roadmap: **Round 1:** the 16-sentence Decoder table (the same one as in L2).
**Round 2:** 12 rapid-fire sentences with no pattern column to lean on.
**Round 3:** "Who breaks the rule?" Pick the situation(s) that make the rule false.
magic: ⬅️ LEFT: if · whenever · provided · the sufficient thing.
➡️ RIGHT: then · only if · the necessary thing · after "implies".
"B if A", "necessary", and whenever/provided in the middle flip the order. "A only if B" never flips, but "Only if B, A" (only if at the front) does.
A rule `A ⇒ B` is broken only by A = T, B = F.

blocks.title: Round 1: the Decoder table
blocks.sub: Say the logic and the direction out loud, then reveal. Turn on **Hard mode** to hide the Pattern and Signal columns.

cells.s: **If** you drop the glass, it breaks.
You get a discount **if** you show your student card.
The alarm rings **if** someone opens the door.

cells: "if" → ⬅️ LEFT, even when it comes second

cells.s: **Provided** you finish your homework, you can play.
**Provided** the battery is charged, the phone turns on.
You can post in the forum **only if** you're a member.
You can drive **only if** you have a licence.
Being born in Sydney is **sufficient** for being born in Australia.
A password is **necessary** to log in.
Being a square **implies** being a rectangle.

blocks.title: Round 2: rapid fire
blocks.sub: Mixed order, new sentences. Give the logic **and** the direction.

items.q: "The printer jams whenever the paper is damp."
items.letters: `j` = the printer jams · `m` = the paper is damp
items.why: "Whenever" in the middle: the part after it is the trigger.

items.q: "You can withdraw cash only if your card is valid."
items.letters: `w` = you withdraw cash · `v` = your card is valid

items.q: "Rain is sufficient for the match to be cancelled."
items.letters: `r` = it rains · `c` = the match is cancelled
items.why: The sufficient thing goes on the left.

items.q: "A charger is necessary to keep the laptop running overnight."
items.letters: `n` = the laptop runs overnight · `c` = it has a charger
items.why: The necessary thing goes on the right.

items.q: "Provided the dough has risen, the bread goes in the oven."
items.letters: `r` = the dough has risen · `o` = the bread goes in the oven
items.why: "Provided" at the front = "if" at the front.

items.q: "The screen dims if the battery is low."
items.letters: `d` = the screen dims · `b` = the battery is low
items.why: "If" in the middle → the part after it goes left.

items.q: "Being a prime bigger than 2 implies being odd."
items.letters: `p` = it's a prime bigger than 2 · `o` = it's odd
items.why: Whatever comes after "implies" goes on the right.

items.q: "If the milk smells sour, you throw it out."
items.letters: `s` = the milk smells sour · `t` = you throw it out

items.q: "Only if the light is green may you cross."
items.letters: `g` = the light is green · `c` = you may cross
items.why: "Only if X, Y" = "Y only if X" → `Y ⇒ X`. Here X (green) is read first, so the order flips.

items.q: "The meeting is cancelled if fewer than three people come."
items.letters: `m` = the meeting is cancelled · `f` = fewer than three people come

items.q: "Pressing the red button is sufficient to stop the machine."
items.letters: `p` = you press the red button · `s` = the machine stops

items.q: "Fuel is necessary for the car to start."

blocks.title: Round 3: who breaks the rule?
blocks.sub: An if–then rule breaks only when the if-part happens and the then-part doesn't. A just-in-case rule breaks whenever the two sides differ. Translate first, then find the breaking situation(s).

items.q: Rule: "You can swim only if a lifeguard is on duty." Which situation breaks it?
items.letters: `s` = you swim · `g` = a lifeguard is on duty
items.why: The rule is `s ⇒ g`. Swimming with no lifeguard is the T ⇒ F row.

items.q: Rule: "Whenever the oven is on, the fan runs." Which situation breaks it?
items.letters: `o` = the oven is on · `f` = the fan runs
items.why: The rule is `o ⇒ f`. (a) is fine: the fan may run for other reasons.

items.q: Rule: "A receipt is necessary for a refund." Which situation breaks it?
items.letters: `r` = you get a refund · `c` = you have a receipt
items.why: Necessary → `r ⇒ c`. A refund without a receipt is the T ⇒ F row. (a) is allowed: necessary isn't sufficient.

items.q: Rule: "I'll cook unless I'm tired." Which situation breaks it?
items.why: Unless = if not: `¬t ⇒ k`. Not tired and still not cooking breaks it. Tired days are left open.

items.q: Rule: "The door opens just in case you tap your card." Which situations break it? (Pick all.)
items.letters: `o` = the door opens · `c` = you tap your card
items.why: `o ⇔ c` needs a match. Both mismatches break it.

items.q: Rule: "If you're under 12, you ride free." Which situation breaks it?
items.why: `u ⇒ f` breaks only for an under-12 who had to pay. (b) is a bonus, not a broken promise.

blocks.title: 🧠 What this drill trains
lines: Find the signal word first, then bucket it: LEFT (if, whenever, provided, sufficient) or RIGHT (then, only if, necessary, after implies).
"B if A", "necessary", and whenever/provided in the middle flip the order. "A only if B" never flips. "Only if B, A" at the front does.
To test an if–then rule, look for where the if-part happens and the then-part doesn't. A just-in-case rule breaks wherever the two sides differ.

sources: All sentences are original. Goes with L2 · If–Then & Friends.
